conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a well-studied set of 10 questions we use with every new parent to check in on mood, anxiety, and overall emotional adjustment during the first year postpartum. Nothing you share today goes beyond this room unless you or baby’s safety is at risk, so please feel comfortable answering honestly. We’ll go one question at a time; each asks how you’ve felt in the past seven days, and we’ll keep the pace relaxed. Ready to begin?

Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, not as much as I used to. I can still laugh if something is really funny, but it feels like it takes more effort—like I have to remind myself to enjoy it instead of it just happening naturally. Maybe a couple of times this week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yes, but it’s definitely harder than before the baby. I laughed once when my husband made a silly joke about diaper explosions, but even then the chuckle felt kind of flat—like I had to push it out rather than it bubbling up on its own.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do find myself looking forward to little things—like the baby’s bath time because he seems so calm in the warm water—but the bigger stuff, like getting coffee with friends or going for a walk, feels more like “I should want to do that” than real excitement. So maybe half the time I feel a spark of enjoyment, and the rest it just feels like another task.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. The baby was fussy for what felt like hours and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset his tummy, or I wasn’t holding him the “right” way. My partner kept saying it’s just what babies do, but I still caught myself wondering if I’d done something to cause it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart races thinking his breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie down at night and picture random scary things—like what if the stroller tips or he rolls off the change table. Nothing’s actually wrong, but the worries just pop in and stick around for a bit before I can talk myself down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times. Once I was just folding laundry and suddenly my chest felt tight and I couldn’t catch my breath—like something awful was about to happen, even though nothing was going on. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky. It’s not every day, but it’s happened maybe two or three times this week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—some days it feels like the minute I finish one thing, the baby needs something else, and the pile of laundry and dishes just keeps growing. I’ll think, “I should be able to handle this,” but by late afternoon I’m running on empty and even little stuff like the doorbell ringing makes me feel like I might snap or cry.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not every night, but a few nights this week I’ve lain there staring at the ceiling even when the baby’s asleep. My mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles right, is he gaining enough weight, will I ever feel like myself again—and I can’t settle. I probably drop off eventually, but it feels like I toss and turn for an hour or more first.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… it comes and goes. I’ll be fine for part of the day, then suddenly feel this wave of sadness—like I’m missing something, or I’m just not cut out for this mom thing. It’s not all day, but I’d say most days this week I’ve had at least one chunk of time where I just feel kind of low and weepy, even if I don’t actually cry.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t actually cried much—maybe once this week. I felt overwhelmed after a night of barely any sleep and the baby wouldn’t settle, and I just teared up while rocking him. It didn’t last long, but it was like the exhaustion and frustration spilled over for a minute.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again, not disappear.

You shared that the early weeks with your baby have felt heavy: laughter comes out flat, activities you "should" enjoy mostly feel like chores, and waves of worry or sadness arrive uninvited. Nights can stretch long with racing thoughts, and ordinary tasks sometimes feel as though they might topple you. At the same time you clearly care deeply for your little one and want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughing is markedly reduced and feels forced, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences noticeably reduced enjoyment for most activities, only occasionally finding small moments of pleasure, aligning best with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a couple of times this week" and gives a specific example of repeatedly faulting herself for the baby's fussiness, fitting "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily intrusive worries about infant safety without cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexpected panic-like episodes (tight chest, breathlessness, dread) occurring 2–3 times in a week; this clearly aligns with "Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent but not constant overwhelm, able to function but with notable strain—best fits "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple nights of difficulty falling asleep due to racing, anxious thoughts—fits "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports experiencing noticeable sadness on most days this week, fitting "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 18 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating high likelihood of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>, supported by <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>daily sadness</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic symptoms</sym>, and <sym>initial insomnia</sym> (DSM-5 criteria: ≥5 symptoms daily for two weeks causing impairment). Absence of self-harm thoughts is noted and protective. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> to review these results
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for comprehensive evaluation and treatment planning
3. Begin basic self-care supports: short outdoor walks, balanced snacks every few hours, brief breathing or grounding exercises when anxiety spikes
4. Ask partner or trusted adult to handle one night-feed so you can obtain a 4-5-hour stretch of uninterrupted sleep
5. Keep 24/7 crisis numbers handy (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and seek emergency care if any thoughts of self-harm or harm to baby emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (partner present) – 1–2 weeks post-delivery

A. Endorsed Symptoms  
• Anhedonia / reduced pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
• Daily low mood, weepy spells (Q8, Q9)  
• Sleep-onset difficulty linked to ruminating worries (Q7)  
• Excessive guilt/blaming self when baby fusses (Q3)  
• Marked “overwhelm,” feels tasks unmanageable, easily tearful (Q6)  
• Recurrent anxious intrusive thoughts (breathing, safety) nearly daily (Q4)  
• Two discrete panic-like episodes this week (tight chest, breathlessness) without clear trigger (Q5)

B. Pattern Summary  
Persistent dysphoric mood with loss of enjoyment, prominent anxiety features, and functional strain; no psychotic content; no self-harm ideation (Q10 denied).

C. Screening Significance  
Scores suggest moderate–high likelihood of postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; meets several EPDS item flags (items 3–9 positive). Absence of self-harm is documented; partner supportive.

D. Recommendations for Clinician  
1. Arrange same-week EPDS formal scoring and clinical interview for PPD/PPA.  
2. Provide psycho-education on postpartum mood/anxiety disorders and local support resources.  
3. Discuss sleep hygiene, respite options, and brief cognitive-behavioral strategies while awaiting evaluation.  
4. Safety: Reinforce 24/7 crisis line; instruct to seek urgent care if any self-harm or infant-harm thoughts emerge.

E. Next Steps  
Referral to OB/midwife and perinatal mental-health specialty; follow-up within 1 week to reassess symptom trajectory and treatment readiness.
